item.title: AVS and benefits: cantonal compensation fund
item.description: How the cantonal compensation fund works for the AVS, the calculation of the pension and supplementary benefits for those who have contribution gaps.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Cantonal compensation fund manages the first pillar AVS locally - Contribution gaps reduce the pension proportionally to the missing years - Supplementary benefits ensure the minimum living standard - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% with employer)
## Key facts - **What**: AVS system with cantonal compensation fund - Where: Each Swiss canton manages its own fund - Who: Federal UFAS/BSV coordinates; cantonal fund applies - Legal basis: First pillar of mandatory pension - Function: Pension calculation, gap management, supplementary benefits
The cantonal compensation fund is the local body that concretely administers the first pillar of Swiss pension. Each canton, from Zurich to Geneva, from Bern to Ticino, has a fund that collects the mandatory contributions of employed workers and coordinates the calculation of future pensions. This multi-level system — federal, cantonal, communal — ensures that those who have paid regularly throughout their career receive an adequate pension, while those with contribution gaps can access supplementary benefits to guarantee the minimum living standard.
The contributions paid each month on the pay slip amount to 5.3% for the employee (with the employer paying an additional 5.3%, for a total of 10.6% according to federal rates). These funds flow into the compensation fund of the canton of residence of the worker, where they are recorded year by year in the individual archive. The fund does not set the rates autonomously — this is the competence of the UFAS/BSV at the federal level — but rigorously applies the national regulation, calculating case by case.
### The administrative role of the cantonal fund
In addition to collecting contributions, the compensation fund performs three key functions. First: it maintains a complete archive of the contribution career of each person, recording year by year the amount of the determining income and the corresponding contributions paid. Second: it coordinates with the funds of other cantons when a worker changes location (for example, moves from Zurich to Lugano) or works temporarily abroad, ensuring continuity of the national contribution path. Third: it manages the calculation of the initial pension and, if necessary, access to supplementary benefits.
When a worker reaches the reference age (65 years for men, 64 for women, subject to legislative changes), the fund receives the pension request and proceeds with the final calculation based on the accumulated contribution career. If gaps emerge during this process — years without payments or with insufficient payments — the fund documents them and communicates to the applicant the impact on the final pension. It is at this stage that the possibility of voluntary buy-backs or access to supplementary benefits comes into play.
The cantonal compensation fund offers individualized consulting services. The advisory role is important because it allows the future retiree to understand exactly how their career influences the pension, and if there are margins for intervention (buy-backs, credits for care periods or unemployment, etc.). ## Contributory gaps: what they are and how they affect you
A contributory gap is a year in which the worker has not paid AVS contributions or has paid them insufficiently. The causes can be multiple: unemployment not covered by insurance, periods of inactivity, income below the minimum contribution threshold (currently very low, but communicated year by year by the fund), or periods spent abroad without international coverage. Each year of gap proportionally reduces the final pension: if the complete professional career would cover 44 years and only 42 are present, the pension will be calculated on 42/44 of the maximum base.
The calculation of the AVS pension follows a standardized national formula, defined by the federal UFAS/BSV but applied locally by the cantonal compensation fund. The formula takes into account the average annual income recorded throughout the career (with adjustments for inflation), multiplied by the number of actual contributory years. It is not a simple division: years of higher income weigh proportionally more, precisely to reflect the insurance concept of the first pillar.
### Mechanisms for covering gaps
Not all gaps are equal from a regulatory point of view. Federal law provides automatic credits for socially relevant periods: years in which one has been a parent of minor children (credits for childcare), periods of compensated unemployment, or years of disability coverage. These credits do not reduce the final pension, as the law considers them "equivalent" to actual payments. The cantonal fund automatically identifies these periods in the contributory career extract.
For residual gaps not covered by credits, the law allows voluntary buy-backs. The applicant can pay a lump sum (calculated by the fund based on the missing years) to retroactively fill the gap. This is a useful option in the years preceding retirement, especially for those who have underestimated the future cost of years of inactivity. However, not all periods are buyable (for example, very remote periods of casual work are often not).
### Supplementary benefits to cover the minimum living standard
When the calculated AVS pension — even after buy-backs — does not reach the federally defined minimum living standard, the compensation fund intervenes with supplementary benefits. This is not social assistance, but a structural element of the first pillar: anyone who has paid for at least one year is entitled to a basic pension, and if this is insufficient, the State guarantees the minimum.
The minimum living standard is set at the federal level (it includes housing, food, utilities, health insurance) but is administratively managed by the cantonal fund according to uniform criteria. Once the pension request is approved, the fund automatically verifies if an integration is necessary. It does not require an additional application: the verification is procedural. However, the applicant must communicate any other income or assets (e.g., real estate beyond the first home), as supplementary benefits take into account the overall asset situation.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to check your contribution status
The first step is to request a contribution history extract from your cantonal compensation fund. This document, available online or on paper request, lists year by year from the first payment to the current year: the recorded determining income, the contributions paid, and any recognized credits or documented gaps. There is no cost to obtain this extract. The fund is obligated to provide it within reasonable times (usually 2-4 weeks, sometimes online in the personal portal of the contributor).
By reading the extract, you can check if there are years with zero amount (pure gaps) or years with amounts lower than the minimum (partial contribution). The fund notes next to each gap the recognized reason (e.g., "period of compensated unemployment, equivalent credit") or "pure gap". This distinction is crucial: equivalent gaps do not reduce the pension, pure gaps do.
### Step-by-step procedure towards retirement
Phase 1 (4-5 years before retirement age): Request the contribution history extract. If non-equivalent gaps emerge, evaluate with the fund whether it is convenient to make voluntary buybacks in the next years.
Phase 2 (about 6-8 months before): The fund, automatically or upon request, provides an indicative estimate of the pension, possibly with the integration of complementary benefits. In this phase, it is still possible to modify buybacks.
Phase 3 (4-6 weeks before the retirement birthday): Submit the formal pension application, equipped with an identity document, bank account extract (for credit), marriage certificate if married (for survivorship). The fund specifies the required documentation in its form.
Phase 4 (within 2-3 months of the application): The fund notifies the final decision with the monthly amount, start date, and possible integration. If the pension is integrated by complementary benefits, the total contribution and the amount available for the minimum living are also communicated.
### Organizational aspects and coordination
AVS contributions continue to be paid regularly even during unemployment, because the unemployment insurance fund (AD) and the insolvency compensation fund (AC) pay the AVS contributions on behalf of the unemployed (up to 1.1% annually up to a maximum, according to federal rates). It is essential to immediately communicate any interruption of work to the cantonal fund, otherwise the payments risk stopping and creating an unjustified gap.
If during the career you have worked in more cantons, the fund of the current canton coordinates with the others to reconstruct the complete national path. This does not cause any delay: the system is computerized and the funds exchange data within a few weeks. It is not necessary to make manual requests between funds.
Use the [AVS pension and minimum living estimate calculator](nav:pension) to get a preliminary idea of the amount, or consult [the tax and pension calculation tool](nav:calculator) for a more complete simulation of your pension and asset situation.

item.title: External Appenzello Driving License: Conversion and Exams
item.description: How to convert the foreign license to External Appenzell: theoretical, practical exam, courses and procedure at the Cantonal Traffic Office.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Foreign driving license conversion in Appenzell Ausserrhoden: procedure regulated at the cantonal level - Theoretical and practical exams mandatory if there is no agreement between countries - Driving courses and practical lessons prepare for the final exam
## Key facts - **What**: Conversion of foreign driving license in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden - Who: Cantonal Traffic Office (Verkehrsbüro) - Where: Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, north-east region of Switzerland - Procedure: Theoretical + practical exam for non-Swiss licenses without bilateral agreements - Courses: Mandatory driving lessons at an authorized driving school - Deadline: Procedure to be completed according to cantonal timelines - Exam languages: Available in German, French, Italian, and Romansh
Anyone moving their residence to Switzerland from a foreign country faces a series of administrative tasks. Among these, the conversion of the driving license represents a crucial phase to continue driving legally on Swiss territory. In the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, as in all Swiss cantons, the procedure follows precise rules defined at the cantonal level.
The conversion of the foreign license begins at the Cantonal Traffic Office (Verkehrsbüro), the entity responsible for managing all road documentation and driving permits. The first step is to submit the conversion application, accompanied by specific documentation: the original license issued by the country of origin, a valid identity document, and a copy of the Swiss residence permit.
### The issue of bilateral agreements
Not all countries have license recognition agreements with Switzerland. If your document was issued in a country that has signed a bilateral agreement with the Confederation (such as many European countries), the Traffic Office can proceed with an administrative conversion without requiring new exams. Otherwise, or if the license is more than two years old, it is mandatory to take the theoretical and practical exams.
### Theoretical and practical exam
The theoretical exam covers knowledge of Swiss traffic regulations and road safety. It is available in multiple languages. The same Cantonal Traffic Office provides information on the date and location of the test.
The practical exam, on the other hand, takes place on real roads, under the supervision of a certified examiner. This test evaluates driving ability in real conditions, adherence to traffic rules, and safety in traffic.
Before taking both exams, Swiss regulations require attending a course at an authorized driving school. It is not possible to take the exams without completing the mandatory driving lessons. ### The practical impact of the cantonal conversion
The procedure for converting your driver's license is not immediate. From the moment you submit your application to the Road Traffic Office until you receive your new Swiss driver's license, it can take weeks or months, depending on the office's workload and your specific situation.
For those coming from an EU/EFTA country (such as Germany, Italy, France), the process is generally more straightforward: the Road Traffic Office often proceeds with an administrative conversion without additional exams, provided that the driver's license is valid and not revoked. You will still need to submit the official application and the required documentation.
For those arriving from non-EU countries, the path is different: both theoretical and practical exams are mandatory, which involves significant effort. Theoretical preparation requires specific study of Swiss regulations (available in manuals provided by the cantonal offices). Practical preparation, on the other hand, involves lessons at a driving school.
### Economic aspects and timelines
The costs of the entire procedure vary by canton. Driving schools charge their own rates for driving lessons, the Road Traffic Office charges fees for the application and issuance of the new driver's license, and examiners have rates for practical tests. In total, you should expect a non-negligible expense; for precise amounts, consult our [guide to the cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland and contact the Road Traffic Office or a local driving school in Appenzell Ausserrhoden directly.
As for the timelines, these also vary. A local driving school can provide details on how many lessons are typically needed to prepare for the practical exam. The exact number depends on your previous experience.
### The role of the Road Traffic Office
The Road Traffic Office of Appenzell Ausserrhoden is the hub of the entire procedure. Here you can submit your initial application, receive all the instructions regarding exams, dates, and required documentation, and arrange for the appointment for the tests. Contacting the Office by phone, email, or in person (if available) is the first fundamental step, even before enrolling in a driving school.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to proceed: the practical checklist
The conversion of the driving license follows some logical steps. Here is the essential procedure.
Step 1: Gather the documentation
Before presenting yourself to the Road Traffic Office, prepare: - Original driving license (or certified copy) - Valid identity document (passport or identity card) - Swiss residence certificate (sometimes required by the office) - Possible clearance from the country of origin (if required)
Step 2: Contact the Road Traffic Office
Appenzell Ausserrhoden has a cantonal Road Traffic Office. Contact them to verify if your license is recognizable for administrative conversion, receive the official application form, request the list of authorized driving schools, and schedule the date for submitting the application.
Step 3: Enroll in a driving school (if necessary)
If the practical exam is mandatory, enroll in an authorized driving school in the canton. Prepare driving lessons according to the recommended program, which usually includes a theoretical and practical component on the road.
Step 4: Take the theoretical exam
The exam takes place at a dedicated location (usually at the Road Traffic Office or at an authorized exam center). After passing this phase, you can access the practical exam.
Step 5: Take the practical exam
Once eligible in the theoretical exam, a certified examiner will guide you in a road driving session. You must demonstrate technical competence and respect for the rules.
Step 6: Receive the Swiss driving license
Once both exams are passed, the Road Traffic Office will issue your Swiss driving license. Delivery times vary depending on cantonal procedures.
### What to expect in practice
There is no strict deadline to complete the entire procedure from the initial application to the final license. Times vary depending on the workload of the cantonal Road Traffic Office and your specific situation.
Throughout the process, the Road Traffic Office remains your main point of reference. Some cantonal offices also offer support through online portals, where you can track the status of your application.
**Next step**: Contact the Road Traffic Office of Appenzell Ausserrhoden directly with your documentation and your specific situation. Each case is unique, and the office will tell you exactly what you need. To explore other aspects of life in Switzerland, consult our [guide to the cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and [job opportunities](nav:jobs).

item.title: Opening a business in Appenzello Esterno: a practical guide
item.description: Legal forms, registration, minimum capital, federal and cantonal taxes, social security and insurance obligations to start a business.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three legal forms: sole proprietorship, simple partnership, public limited company - Mandatory registration in the cantonal commercial register - Federal, cantonal, and municipal tax and social security obligations - Social security: AHV/IV (5.3%), ALV/UVG (1.1%), mandatory health insurance (LAMal)
## Key facts - **What**: Starting a business requires federal, cantonal, and municipal compliance - Where: Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden (northeastern Switzerland) - Who: Entrepreneurs, self-employed, small and medium-sized enterprises - Competence: Cantonal offices for commercial register and cantonal taxes; federal offices for AHV/LPP and VAT - Requirements: Legal form, variable minimum capital, mandatory insurances
Starting a business in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden requires compliance with a series of federal, cantonal, and municipal obligations. Choosing the legal form is the first step: sole proprietorship, simple partnership, or public limited company, each with different implications for minimum capital, taxation, and personal liability.
Registration in the cantonal commercial register is mandatory for most businesses. This administrative requirement is handled by the competent cantonal offices and must be completed before starting operations.
Simultaneously, those starting a business must comply with federal, cantonal, and municipal tax obligations. The Swiss tax system operates on three distinct levels: the federal direct tax (BST) managed by the FTA (Federal Tax Administration), cantonal taxes managed by the competent cantonal office, and municipal taxes calculated with a multiplier on the cantonal value. Each canton, including Appenzell Ausserrhoden, has its own laws and rates.
Self-employed individuals and small business owners are required to contribute to the federal social security system. The Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AHV) and Disability Insurance (IV) require a 5.3% contribution from the self-employed, with an additional employer component (total 10.6%). Contributions to Unemployment Insurance (ALV) and Insolvency Insurance (UVG) amount to a total of 1.1% up to an annually determined federal maximum.
Regarding mandatory occupational pension provision (BVG), self-employed individuals are not directly obliged, but many choose to voluntarily join pension funds to ensure a pension in case of disability or old age.
[Health insurance LAMal](nav:health) is mandatory for all residents of Switzerland, including the self-employed. This is a private insurance with per capita premiums, not a wage tax or federal contribution. Each canton defines premium bands and possible cantonal reductions (subsidies).
### Choosing the legal form
The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: the owner is unlimitedly liable, and minimum capital is typically not required (depends on the sector). The simple partnership requires at least two partners and does not require minimum capital. The public limited company (AG) requires a minimum capital of CHF 20,000 (payable for at least 20% at the time of foundation), subjects the company to mandatory auditing, and limits the liability of the partners. ### Cantonal tax and administrative implications The canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, like all Swiss cantons, manages its own cantonal tax regime and sets the framework for municipal taxes. This means that the effective tax rate varies depending on the municipality within the canton. Self-employed individuals and entrepreneurs must file their cantonal and municipal tax returns annually with the cantonal administration. The direct federal tax is managed at the federal level by the FTA, but it is calculated based on a federal rate that is uniform across Switzerland, except for progressivity. For small growing businesses, VAT (Value Added Tax) becomes relevant when the turnover exceeds certain annual thresholds set at the federal level. The FTA manages all VAT-related issues at the national level. An important aspect for self-employed individuals operating from a base in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden is the distinction between: - Direct federal taxes (DFT): a progressive tax managed by the FTA - Cantonal taxes: managed by the competent cantonal office, with specific rates for the canton - Municipal taxes: calculated as a multiplier of the cantonal amount, varying between municipalities within the same canton Self-employed individuals should also register with the social security registry at the competent federal office (UFAS/BSV). This office does not set the taxes but coordinates the payment of AVS/AI/AD/AC contributions and manages pension rights. Registration must occur within specific times from the start of the activity to avoid administrative penalties. ### Insurance obligations beyond the LAMal In addition to mandatory health insurance, many entrepreneurs voluntarily subscribe to professional insurances: liability insurance, accident insurance (although partially covered by LAA/LAINF for employers), disability insurance, and life insurance. SUVA, a federal para-fiscal institution, manages accident insurance for employed workers and, in certain sectors, also for self-employed individuals with employees. Those who have employees must insure them with SUVA (if the employer has sites in sectors subject to SUVA obligation) or with authorized private insurers. LAINF/LAA contributions start from approximately 0.7% up to 1.5% of the coordinated salary, depending on the sector of activity. The payment of these contributions is part of the fixed costs of the company and must be planned from the early stages of business growth.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical procedure to open a business in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden
Step 1: Choosing the legal form Before taking any action, decide whether to operate as a sole proprietorship, simple partnership, or corporation. Consult a notary or tax advisor to understand the implications of minimum capital, personal liability, and administrative burdens.
Step 2: Registration with the cantonal commercial register The commercial register of the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden requires the registration of any commercial, craft, or agricultural activity that employs staff or generates revenue above a certain threshold (for sole proprietorships). Contact the competent cantonal office (State Chancellery or cantonal commercial register office) for specific details and forms. Registration is done on an official form and generally involves a registration fee, the amount of which varies depending on the canton and legal form.
Step 3: Federal tax registration If the turnover exceeds federal thresholds, the company must register with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA) for VAT and federal direct tax. The FTA provides unique identification numbers (tax number, VAT number).
Step 4: Cantonal tax registration Register with the competent cantonal office for cantonal and municipal taxes. The Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden has specific procedures; the cantonal office will guide you through the necessary steps.
**Step 5: Health insurance (LAMal)** Take out health insurance with an authorized insurer. LAMal is mandatory for all residents of Switzerland within 3 months of starting the activity (if not previously insured).
Step 6: Social security registration (AHV/IV) Register with the competent cantonal office to pay AHV/IV contributions as a self-employed person. The UFAS/BSV coordinates these registrations at the federal level.
Step 7: Possible SUVA registration (if you employ staff) If you hire employees, register them with SUVA or with an authorized private insurer for accident insurance (LAINF/LAA).
This procedure ensures compliance with federal, cantonal, and municipal requirements. The total implementation time varies but generally takes 2-4 weeks, provided the documentation is complete.
### Available tools and resources
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to understand the social security and tax burdens on potential employees you intend to hire. Consult the [tax return form](nav:tax-return) for declaration forms and specific deadlines for the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

item.title: Opening a business in Appenzello Esterno: procedures and costs
item.description: Complete guide: legal forms, trade register, minimum capital, AVS/LPP contributions and insurance obligations to set up a business in the canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three legal forms: sole proprietorship, LLC (CHF 20,000), corporation (CHF 100,000) - Mandatory registration in the cantonal commercial register - Mandatory contributions to AHV/AI/LPP and health insurance - Three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, and municipal
## Key facts - **What**: Registering a business in the canton - Who: Tax authorities and cantonal registry offices - Where: Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden - Available forms: Sole proprietorship, LLC, corporation - Requirements: Mandatory registration, pension contributions, LAMal
Opening a business in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden involves a series of administrative and tax obligations that vary depending on the chosen legal form. Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage but imposes strict requirements on pensions, health insurance, and registration in the cantonal commercial register. The choice between a sole proprietorship, limited liability company (LLC), or corporation determines both the administrative complexity and the mandatory pension contributions.
### Legal forms and requirements
In Switzerland, those wishing to start a business have three main options. The sole proprietorship does not require a minimum capital and offers maximum administrative simplicity, but the owner is personally liable with their personal assets. It is the natural choice for self-employed professionals, consultants, and independent traders. It is also ideal for those who want to maintain complete managerial autonomy without involving other partners.
The limited liability company (LLC) protects the personal assets of the partners: liability is limited to the share capital, not less than CHF 20,000. This form offers greater credibility towards clients and suppliers compared to the sole proprietorship, but requires slightly more complex administrative management. Each partner contributes their share of capital, which remains deposited with a bank until the official registration.
The corporation represents the most structured form and is required by larger companies or those with institutional investors. The minimum capital is CHF 100,000 and must be paid before registration. The corporation requires a board of directors, a formal statute, and more rigorous accounting.
### Registration in the commercial register
Registration in the commercial register is mandatory in every Swiss canton. In the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, the process involves submitting a dossier to the competent cantonal office. There is no uniform federal deadline — each canton regulates the timing, but generally, registration must occur before or immediately after the start of the activity.
For a sole proprietorship, the essential documents include: certificate of nationality or residence permit, copy of a valid identity document, completed and signed registration form, and possibly a copy of the lease agreement if the premises are rented.
For an LLC or corporation, the documentation is more complex: notarized deed of incorporation, statute, bank certificate of deposit of the minimum capital, complete list of partners and administrators, authenticated signatures. Each canton may add specific requirements — it is therefore essential to contact the cantonal commercial register office before proceeding. Once the activity is registered, the self-employed person is subject to tax obligations at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Each canton — including Appenzell Ausserrhoden — has its own multipliers and rates for cantonal and municipal taxes. The federal direct tax is uniform at the national level but is calculated based on the specific situation of each taxpayer.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Checklist to open a business
Before registering with the commercial register in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, it is useful to prepare a detailed checklist. First: choose the legal form (sole proprietorship, LLC, or corporation) based on the size of the investment, the expected management complexity, and the number of partners. Second: deposit the minimum capital with a Swiss bank (if the chosen form requires it) and obtain the bank deposit certificate. Third: gather personal documentation (certificate of nationality, copy of ID card, and possibly residence permit if foreign).
Fourth: contact the commercial register office of the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden and request the complete registration dossier and specific cantonal instructions. Fifth: complete the registration form in all its parts, sign, and attach all required documents. Sixth: submit the dossier to the office (usually by registered mail, certified email, or in person) and obtain the official receipt of submission.
### Deadlines and next steps
After registering with the commercial register, within three months it is mandatory to register with the cantonal tax office and, in parallel, take out a validated health insurance. There is no single federal registration fee — costs vary significantly by canton and legal form. Each canton charges its own administrative fees for registration with the commercial register.
The tax identification number (UID) is automatically assigned by the cantonal tax office and allows you to start the business for all tax purposes. Ensure that this number appears on every official document and invoice.
For a personalized assessment of the specific tax and social security costs in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, [consult the tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the federal direct tax, then contact the cantonal tax administration and the local commercial register office directly for details on specific cantonal rates and taxes.

item.description: The Canton of Appenzello Outermost manages the first AVS pillar through a cantonal compensation fund, guaranteeing benefits to taxpayers.
item.content:encoded:
## Management of the first pillar AVS in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden
## In brief - The Compensation Fund of the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden administers the AVS, the cornerstone of the Swiss pension system. - Each missing year of contribution reduces the lifelong pension by approximately 1/44. - Supplementary benefits supplement the AVS pension to ensure the minimum living standard. - Pension planning requires constant verification of the individual account statement.
## Key facts - What: Operational management and collection of AVS/AI/IPG contributions. - Where: Herisau, headquarters of the Compensation Fund of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. - Who: Mandatory insured persons and employers of the canton. - Legal basis: Federal Law on Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (LAVS).
The AVS system in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden operates within a strict federal framework. Although the rules are uniform at the national level, interaction with the cantonal office is crucial for managing payments and regularizing gaps.
### Pension calculation and impact of gaps The AVS pension depends on the years of contribution and the average annual income. For 2024, the minimum pension is set at 1,225 francs per month, while the maximum reaches 2,450 francs. A single year of non-contribution, for example, for a period of study abroad not covered, results in a permanent reduction of the pension. Compared to cantons with a higher cost of living, such as Zurich or Geneva, management in Appenzell Ausserrhoden follows the same federal tables, but access to supplementary benefits is adjusted according to the spending limit recognized by the canton.
> Pension planning is not a static event but a dynamic process that requires continuous monitoring.

item.title: Neuchâtel transport subscriptions: zones and fares
item.description: Find out how public transport passes work in the Canton of Neuchâtel: fare zones, half-price, GA and discounts for students and apprentices.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss public transport: zone fare system and national fare communities - Annual, monthly, half-fare and GA passes available in all cantons - Special discounts for students and apprentices with CartaJuventus and school certificates - Ticket validation online, via mobile app or at physical counters
## Key facts - **What**: Public transport passes with zone fare system - Where: Canton of Neuchâtel, Switzerland - When: Current system applicable until 2026 - Who: Regional and federal transport companies (SBB), fare communities - Passes: Annual, monthly, half-fare, unlimited national GA - Discounts: Students and apprentices (CartaJuventus and official certificates)
The Swiss public transport system is organized into fare zones defined by distance and geographical area. In the Canton of Neuchâtel, as in the rest of Switzerland, travelers benefit from a coherent fare structure that simplifies the planning of daily trips.
Fare communities form the basis of the organization of [Swiss public transport](nav:transport). These associations coordinate fares among different operators (regional trains, buses, trams, boats), ensuring fare uniformity and facilitating transfers between different modes of transport without administrative complications. In the Canton of Neuchâtel, the same fare principles and rules apply as in all other Swiss cantons, with zones extending based on the distance traveled.
### How fare zones work
Zones are defined by distance bands: each ticket or pass covers a certain number of zones. A traveler moving within one or two zones pays a lower fare than someone covering greater distances. This system encourages the purchase of passes for regular trips and reduces the overall cost of mobility in the medium to long term.
Annual passes represent the most cost-effective solution for daily commuters, while monthly passes offer flexibility for those with periodic mobility needs. Both operate on a zone basis: an "1 zone annual" pass covers all trips within a specific zone for the entire calendar year, while a "2-3 zone" pass allows for longer distances. ### Half-price, GA and fare combinations
The national half-price (Halbtax/Demi-tarif) is a subscription that reduces by 50% all subsequent tickets purchased. Many Swiss travelers choose to activate the half-price (at a fixed annual cost) because the savings quickly amortize with a few trips. In the Canton of Neuchâtel, the half-price combines with any regional subscription and works on all lines operated by the local fare community.
The GA (General-Abonnement) is the most ambitious unlimited subscription: it allows you to travel freely on ALL Swiss public transport (trains, buses, trams, boats, cable cars in many regions) without geographical zone limits. Those who own a GA do not need to purchase additional tickets for any national journey. In the Canton of Neuchâtel, the GA represents a solution for those who travel frequently both within the canton and to other Swiss regions (for work, study, leisure, business).
The combination of half-price + zonal subscription is very common: the traveler purchases the annual subscription for their main travel zone (home-work) and activates the half-price for occasional trips beyond that zone. Some travelers choose the GA alone if their trips are intense and varied across the entire Swiss territory, considering that the GA offers cost predictability and eliminates the problem of fare choice.
### Discounts for students and apprentices
Students enrolled in middle, high, and university schools benefit from specific reductions through the CartaJuventus (Swiss youth card). This card allows the purchase of discounted tickets (generally 25-50% discount) on zonal subscriptions and on individual trips. Apprentices following professional training programs (AFP/CFC) have access to the same discounts, provided they are registered with the training company and the official educational institution.
To take advantage of the discounts, students and apprentices must present a registration certificate (school document or apprenticeship certificate) at the counter where they purchase the subscription. Many cantons, including Neuchâtel, allow the activation of discounts also through a dedicated app, where the student status is digitally verified by the educational institution.
The concrete savings on mobility quickly add up: a monthly subscription with CartaJuventus can cost 30-40% less than the standard price, resulting in significant savings for those who travel frequently during the academic year. This reduces the overall [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) for students and apprentices, making public mobility more accessible and supporting participation in education and professional training.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Purchase and validation procedure in 5 steps
Step 1: Identify the main travel zone. Consult the zone map on the cantonal transport company's website or via the app. The zones are numbered and color-coded for easy reading. In the Canton of Neuchâtel, most commuters travel within 2-3 zones.
Step 2: Choose the type of subscription. If the trips are daily (home-work, home-school), an annual subscription is the most economical solution. If the trips are occasional or sporadic, a monthly subscription is better. Evaluate whether the half-price ticket is convenient based on your mobility habits.
Step 3: Check the requirements for discounts. If you are a student or apprentice, prepare the official enrollment certificate. If you intend to purchase a CartaJuventus, check the maximum age (usually up to 25 years) and eligibility based on the type of school or training.
**Step 4: Purchase the subscription.** The options are: - Online through the cantonal transport company's portal (faster, with paper or digital delivery) - At the main station counter (direct assistance, immediate validation) - Through the official mobile app (for digital subscriptions, instant validation)
Step 5: Validate the ticket before each trip. Depending on the type of subscription: - Paper subscription: swipe the card in the validator installed on board the vehicle - Digital subscription (app): show the ticket on the smartphone screen to the inspector - CartaJuventus: present the physical card or the digital QR code during the check
### When and where to buy conveniently
Buying subscriptions online is generally more convenient because early-bird promotions (if purchased in advance) or multi-year discounts are often available. The main stations of the Canton of Neuchâtel (La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle, Neuchâtel city) have dedicated counters where staff can advise on the type of subscription best suited to the individual mobility profile.
The start date of the subscription is flexible: it can be activated on any day of the month, not necessarily the 1st. This allows you to align the purchase with your mobility needs (for example, activate a monthly subscription from the 15th of the month if you know that the trips will be intense only from the 15th onwards). The flexibility in managing activation dates represents a practical advantage for those with variable needs.
### Save with the mobility calculator
To compare the different subscription options, calculate the cost of your average monthly trip and understand whether it is convenient to choose the half-price ticket, the GA, or a simple zonal subscription, use the [salary and cost of living calculator](nav:calculator) of Frontaliere Ticino. You can enter your canton of residence and view the total mobility cost in relation to your income and travel needs. This way, you can identify the most convenient subscription option and plan your mobility budget for the year, maximizing savings.

item.title: Buying a house in Neuchâtel: prices and mortgage
item.description: Buying a house in Neuchâtel: calculation of own funds, sustainable mortgage, transfer taxes and notary fees in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Own funds require at least 20% of the purchase price - The mortgage is sustainable if it does not exceed 450% of the annual gross income - The transfer tax is due to the Canton of Neuchâtel - Notary fees vary depending on the value of the property
## Key facts - **What**: Acquisition of real estate in the Canton of Neuchâtel - Where: Canton of Neuchâtel, French-speaking Switzerland - Who: Resident buyers, Swiss banks, cantonal notaries - Own funds: Minimum 20% of the purchase price - Maximum mortgage: Up to 450% of annual gross income - Cantonal taxes: Transfer tax + notary fees - Institution: SNB determines base interest rates
Buying a house in the Canton of Neuchâtel requires careful financial planning and understanding of the total costs involved. The Swiss real estate market, including Neuchâtel, is based on a standardized financing system at the national level, where banks and credit institutions apply sustainability criteria recognized throughout the country.
In the Swiss system, the fundamental rule for obtaining a mortgage loan is that the buyer must have own funds corresponding to at least 20% of the purchase price. This minimum level is a well-established norm among major Swiss financial institutions, whether they are cantonal banks, universal banks, or real estate leasing companies. Having own funds greater than 20% allows for negotiating better interest rates and reduces the overall debt burden.
The Canton of Neuchâtel, like all Swiss cantons, applies its own tax regime for the transfer of real estate. In addition to own funds and the mortgage, the buyer must plan for the payment of the transfer tax (also known as the transfer tax), a cantonal tax on the transfer of property, as well as notary fees for the drafting of the purchase deed.
The Swiss National Bank (SNB), through the setting of reference interest rates, directly influences the mortgage rates offered by the market. Although the SNB does not directly set residential mortgage rates (which remain the responsibility of private banks), its monetary policy orientation has a decisive impact on the cost of money in Switzerland. A buyer planning to purchase a property in Neuchâtel must consider both the current cost of the mortgage and possible future variations.
An honest assessment of one's financial situation is essential before starting the purchase process. Calculating available own funds, reviewing annual repayment capacity, and projecting monthly mortgage costs are crucial steps to avoid taking on unsustainable debt. ## How to assess the sustainability of a mortgage
In the Swiss system, credit institutions apply standardized rules to determine whether a mortgage is sustainable for the borrower. The most common rule is the so-called 450% ratio: the total mortgage should not exceed 450% of the borrower's (or couple's, if married and with combined incomes) gross annual income. This rule represents a well-established standard in the Swiss banking sector and aims to protect both the lender and the borrower from taking on excessive obligations.
For example, in a hypothetical scenario: if the gross annual income is CHF 100,000, the sustainable mortgage should not exceed CHF 450,000. Naturally, other factors influence this assessment, such as existing debts, number of dependents, and variability of income over time.
The Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio is another fundamental parameter. If you purchase a property for CHF 500,000 and have own funds of CHF 100,000 (20%), the mortgage will be CHF 400,000, with an LTV of 80%. Swiss banks and mortgage insurers generally offer more favorable rates for LTV up to 80%; beyond this level, additional mortgage insurance may be required.
The impact of professional pension provision (LPP, second pillar) and old-age insurance (AVS, first pillar) must be considered in long-term planning. The sustainability of a mortgage must also be verified in light of the future ability to repay it after retirement, when contributions to the pension system will decrease or cease. Institutions such as UFAS/BSV manage the pension criteria, while each canton (including Neuchâtel) applies common norms at the federal level.
### The role of monthly fixed costs
Every mortgage involves monthly fixed costs, calculated based on the amount borrowed, the duration of the financing (typically 15-25 years for Swiss mortgages) and the interest rate. An increase in interest rates (which depends on the decisions of the SNB and global economic conditions) results in an increase in future monthly costs, especially if the mortgage is at a variable rate or in the renegotiation phase.
Buyers should calculate the total cost of living: mortgage + interest + municipal property taxes + insurance premiums (fire, liability) + ordinary and extraordinary maintenance. This total, compared to available income, determines the real financial burden. A careful simulation allows avoiding surprises and verifying compatibility with the family budget in the medium to long term.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Administrative costs and the purchase procedure
Buying a property in Neuchâtel involves administrative and tax costs in addition to the purchase price and mortgage interest. The Canton of Neuchâtel, as part of Switzerland, applies a property transfer tax (stamp duty). The exact amount varies according to the specific cantonal and municipal legislation of Neuchâtel and can be applied as a percentage of the transfer value or as a fixed amount according to predetermined brackets. We recommend contacting the tax administration of the Canton of Neuchâtel directly to obtain precise information on the applicable rate.
Notary fees in Switzerland are regulated at the cantonal level and vary according to the value of the property. The notary in charge of drafting the purchase deed (and subsequent registration in the land register) charges a fee proportional to the value of the transaction. It is advisable to request quotes from several notaries before proceeding, as there may be price variations within certain limits.
In addition to the mortgage, stamp duty, and notary fees, the buyer must budget for: mortgage insurance (sometimes mandatory if the LTV exceeds 80%), property valuation (required by the bank before granting the mortgage), land register registration costs (managed by the competent office in the canton), and any municipal transfer or registration taxes.
### Step-by-step procedure
The purchase procedure follows a standardized scheme in Switzerland:
1. Negotiation and preliminary agreement: The buyer and seller reach a verbal agreement on the price and main conditions.
2. Bank appraisal: The bank assesses the sustainability of the mortgage according to national criteria, requests the property appraisal, and verifies the client's financial situation.
3. Mortgage offer letter: The bank communicates the amount, interest rate, and conditions of the mortgage within a defined period.
4. Appointment of the notary: The parties appoint the notary to draft the sales contract and manage the legal procedure for transferring the property.
5. Land register registration: After signing, the notary proceeds with the registration of the property in the name of the new owner at the competent office of the canton.
6. Mortgage disbursement: The bank disburses the financing once the formalities are completed and the final documents are obtained.
For a correct assessment of your repayment capacity, it is advisable to use a [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) that allows you to simulate different interest rate and loan duration scenarios. Understanding the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and your tax situation is equally important: an [accurate tax return](nav:tax-return) ensures maximum transparency towards the authorities and the lender.

item.title: Wages and work in Schaffhausen: sectors, training, levels
item.description: Wages in the Schaffhausen: levels for training, collective agreements and social contributions in the Swiss system.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Switzerland has no federal minimum wage; some cantons have their own - Salary levels depend on education, sector, and collective agreements - Mandatory social contributions: AVS/AI 5.3%, LPP 7% to 18% - Maximum working hours 45-50 hours/week; minimum 4 weeks vacation
## Key facts
- **What**: Swiss salary determination system based on education, sector, and collective agreements - When: Current system; amounts indexed annually - Where: All cantons, including Schaffhausen - Who: Employees in the private, public, and semi-public sectors - Regulation: Federal labor law, cantonal ordinances, collective agreements - Working hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales); 50 hours other sectors - Vacation: Minimum 4 weeks; 5 weeks until age 20
### The Swiss system: no federal minimum wage
Switzerland is one of the few European countries without a mandatory federal minimum wage. This means that the Canton of Schaffhausen, like every other canton, determines autonomously whether and what minimum wage to set. Some Swiss cantons have introduced their own cantonal minimum wage; others do not. Salary determination follows criteria related to professional training, experience, and collective labor agreements (CCL), which regulate salaries for sector and profession.
In Switzerland, the labor market recognizes three main levels of education: vocational training with a federal certificate (EFA), high school diploma (which allows access to university), and university education (bachelor and master). Each level corresponds to different salary scales. A professional with EFA earns on average less than someone with a high school diploma, who in turn earns less than a degree holder. The differences are not fixed but vary by sector.
Collective agreements are the main tool for salary regulation. Negotiated between unions and employers' associations, CCLs set minimum wages, seniority increases, benefits, and working conditions for entire sectors (construction, trade, industry, public services, etc.). In the Canton of Schaffhausen, as in every canton, the current CCLs reflect local compromises between trade unions and business organizations.
### Working hours and vacations
The federal labor law sets the maximum working hours at 45 hours per week for the industrial, office, and sales sectors, and at 50 hours for other sectors. The minimum vacation is four weeks per year for adults, rising to five weeks until age 20. These limits apply uniformly in all cantons. ### Salary differences by level of education and sector
The Swiss job market rewards education, but the starting salary of a new hire also depends on the sector. Manufacturing, finance, technology, and healthcare tend to offer higher salaries. Retail, hospitality, and agriculture generally pay less. In Schaffhausen, as in the rest of Switzerland, traditional economic sectors (industry, craftsmanship) remain important, and wages follow national levels for their branch.
A generic scenario illustrates the differences: a new hire with a Federal Vocational Baccalaureate (FVB) in the manufacturing sector receives a base salary linked to the collective labor agreement (CLA) of their branch, possibly increased by performance bonuses. Those who have completed a high school diploma can access administrative or technical positions with higher salaries. A university graduate generally starts with an even higher salary, although this depends on the specialization and sector. However, these differences are not automatic: a graduate in a poorly paid sector (e.g., cultural animation) might earn less than a specialized FVB technician in a high-demand sector (e.g., construction).
### Pay slip structure: contributions and deductions
The [Swiss pay slip](nav:payslip) shows the gross salary and all mandatory deductions. The main social contributions are:
- **AVS/AI/IPG**: 5.3% on the gross salary (paid by the employee). The employer contributes an additional 5.3%. - Unemployment insurance (AD): 1.1% up to an annual maximum. - Accident insurance (LAA/LAINF): 0.7–1.5% depending on the sector (paid by the employer; generally not deducted from the pay slip). - Occupational pension scheme (LPP/BVG): 7% (for coordinated salary, age bracket 25–34 years), increasing with age: 10% (35–44 years), 15% (45–54 years), 18% (55+ until retirement age). - Health insurance: Voluntary and private, with premiums varying by canton. It is not a salary deduction but a personal expense.
These amounts are strictly regulated by federal law and cantonal ordinances. The rates are annually indexed, so the exact values vary each year. Anyone reading a Swiss pay slip should expect a significant difference between gross and net due to these mandatory factors.
### Impact of pension scheme on salary
An often underestimated aspect is the weight of the occupational pension scheme (LPP). For an employee between 25 and 34 years old, 7% of the coordinated salary (total salary minus a standard deduction) goes into LPP. This represents a considerable value in the medium to long term, as it forms the basis of the pension benefit. As age advances, the contribution percentage increases, reflecting the concept that those who enter the pension scheme later must contribute higher percentages to achieve an equivalent benefit. Understanding this mechanism helps to truly evaluate the value of a Swiss salary beyond just the monthly net amount.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Informarsi sui salari: dove cercare
Il primo passo per chi entra nel mercato del lavoro svizzero è comprendere la gamma salariale del proprio settore e della propria regione. Esistono diverse risorse pubbliche gratuite:
1. **Portali statistici federali (UST/BFS)**: L'Ufficio federale di statistica pubblica dati annuali su salari medi per branca economica, cantone e livello di formazione. Questi dati sono liberi e riportano la situazione reale del mercato.
2. Contratti collettivi: I CCL sono pubblicati da associazioni sindacali e datoriali. Consultarli prima di accettare un'offerta di lavoro permette di verificare se lo stipendio proposto è conforme ai standard negoziali della branca.
3. Uffici cantonali del lavoro: Nel Canton Sciaffusa, come in ogni cantone, esiste un ufficio cantonale competente per il mercato del lavoro. Questi uffici forniscono informazioni su vigenza di contratti collettivi, salari minimi cantonali (se esistono) e diritti dei lavoratori.
4. Portale nazionale SECO: La Segreteria di Stato dell'economia (SECO) pubblica una banca dati di contratti collettivi vigenti. È possibile cercare per cantone e settore per verificare i termini in vigore.
### Procedura per valutare un'offerta di lavoro
Quando ricevi un'offerta di lavoro in Svizzera, segui questi passaggi:
- Controlla lo stipendio lordo proposto contro i dati UST/BFS e il CCL vigente per il settore. - Chiedi una simulazione della busta paga netta [usando un calcolatore](nav:calculator) (disponibile sul sito) per capire realmente quanto percepirai considerando tutti i contributi. - Verifica i termini di disdetta: il contratto deve rispettare i termini legali (1, 2 o 3 mesi secondo il periodo di impiego già completato). - Leggi con attenzione il contratto per verificare benefit aggiuntivi (orari, flessibilità, bonus, giorni di congedo extra).
Comprendere i livelli salariali svizzeri evita sorprese e consente una negoziazione consapevole. In Sciaffusa, come nel resto della Svizzera, il mercato del lavoro è trasparente e regolato: conoscere le regole conviene.
### Iscriviti per ricevere aggiornamenti
Ogni anno le aliquote contributive, i massimali e i livelli salariali di riferimento vengono aggiornati. Restare informato su questi cambiamenti è importante per monitorare il proprio reddito reale. [Calcola il tuo stipendio netto](nav:calculator) usando il nostro strumento per simulare l'impatto di contributi e tasse sulla tua busta paga e scopri in tempo reale quanto percepirai.

item.title: Wages and the labour market: training, sectors and levels
item.description: The Swiss salary consists of gross, AVS/LPP/LAMal and net contributions. Learn how salaries vary by training, industry, and how to check your paycheck.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - A Swiss salary consists of gross, social contributions, and net - Fixed contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF/LAA 0.7–1.5% - Salaries vary by level of education and sector of activity - Some cantons have a minimum wage; most do not
## Key facts - **What**: Composition of a Swiss salary (gross minus deductions) - When: Deductions applied monthly from each employee's salary - Where: In every Swiss canton, with variations for taxes and subsidies - Who: SECO, UST/BFS, and cantonal administrations manage employment data - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of gross salary (10.6% with employer's contribution) - LPP: 7–18% of coordinated salary depending on age bracket - LAMal: Mandatory private insurance for residents, not deducted from salary
### Gross, contributions, and net: composition of a Swiss salary
When an employee receives a [Swiss payslip](nav:payslip), they do not see the gross salary agreed upon in the contract directly. The transition from gross to net occurs through standardized and mandatory deductions applied monthly.
From each salary, contributions to AVS (old-age insurance), AI (disability insurance), and IPG (loss of earnings allowance) are deducted: the employee contributes a total of 5.3% of the gross salary. This is supplemented by unemployment contributions (AD/AC), amounting to 1.1% up to an annual maximum, and accident insurance contributions (LAINF/LAA), which range from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity.
The occupational pension fund (LPP/BVG) deducts a percentage of the coordinated salary that depends on the employee's age: 7% for those aged 25 to 34, 10% for those aged 35 to 44, 15% for those aged 45 to 54, and 18% for those aged 55 and above until the reference age. This increasing contribution reflects the greater accumulation of pension capital as one approaches retirement.
Swiss health insurance (LAMal) works differently: it is not a salary deduction but a private contract that every resident must sign within three months of arrival. Premiums vary by canton and region, with adult deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2500. In many cantons, those with low incomes are eligible for subsidies to reduce premiums.
Finally, from the amount net of all social contributions, federal direct tax (IFD) is withheld, along with cantonal and communal taxes, which vary significantly depending on the canton of residence and personal tax situation. ### Salaries by level of training and sectors of activity
The Swiss labour market significantly rewards the level of training achieved. Those with a compulsory school diploma (primary/lower secondary education) generally have access to operational positions in sectors such as manufacturing, construction or auxiliary services, with low salaries. A basic vocational training diploma (federal certificate of ability, AFC) or a second cycle secondary qualification opens access to technical, craft or administrative roles, with considerably higher salaries.
Holders of a tertiary diploma-both university (Bachelor/Master) and higher professional (diplomas of university vocational schools, SUPs) -position themselves at the top of the salary distribution, accessing coordination, technical specialization, research or management positions. This wage differential by level of training is structural in the Swiss market.
The sector to which they belong also has a significant impact on wages. Manufacturing, finance, and insurance tend to offer high wages thanks to productivity and operating margins. Retail, hospitality and ancillary services have lower average salaries. Agriculture shows a broad spectrum, but often with lower wages than the advanced tertiary sectors.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to read a Swiss payslip and check your salary
A Swiss payslip transparently shows: the gross contractual salary, the detailed breakdown of all contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA, LPP), the total gross amount from which the contributions are deducted, and finally the net amount paid into the worker's bank account. For Swiss residents, the document also specifies the federal withholding tax, while the cantonal and communal withholdings are calculated based on the annual tax return.
To check if your salary is in line with the market, it is useful to consult the data provided by UST/BFS, which publishes monthly and annual statistics on the salary structure by sector, profession, region, and level of education. If you are classified in a sector covered by a CCT, your specific collective agreement sets the minimum wages for each category: check that your gross amount is not lower than what is provided in the salary table for your professional category and years of seniority.
### Official tools and sources to consult data on salaries and employment
To verify certified information on salaries, employment, and the labor market, refer to these main tools: SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) provides a comprehensive database of collective agreements, employment statistics, and sectoral benchmarks. UST/BFS (Federal Statistical Office) publishes the Salary Structure Survey (ISS), with regional data disaggregated by sector, profession, and level of education. Cantonal administrations provide specific information on cantonal minimum wage (where applicable), LAMal subsidies, and local tax rates. Trade unions and employers' associations allow direct consultation of the specific CCT for your sector and profession.

item.title: Neuchâtel Scholarships: Requirements and Amounts
item.description: Complete guide to scholarships in the Canton of Neuchâtel: award criteria, residency and academic merit requirements, application procedure and where to find updated calls.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Scholarships for deserving students in financial need in the Canton of Neuchâtel - Requirements: cantonal residence, academic merit and economic situation - Maximum amounts and deadlines vary annually: consult official notices - To apply: registration, financial documents, application by deadline
## Key facts - **What**: Scholarships for deserving and economically needy students - Where: Canton of Neuchâtel - Who: Cantonal Office of Education and Training - Main requirements: Cantonal residence, academic merit, analysis of the family economic situation - Frequency: Calls and deadlines vary annually
The Canton of Neuchâtel offers scholarships to students who accumulate academic merit with economic difficulties. Unlike other social aid, training grants are not universal: each Swiss canton decides on its own amounts, criteria and allocation procedure, in compliance with federal principles of equity.
Access to scholarships in the Canton of Neuchâtel passes through an analysis of the economic situation of the student's family. There is no published fixed maximum income: the canton uses an assessment system that considers gross income, deductions for fixed expenses, the number of dependent employees and the cost of living in the cantonal territory.
### Who is entitled?
Residents of the Canton of Neuchâtel attending first level studies (bachelor), second level (master) ### Differences between cantons and impact on student mobility
Scholarships in the Canton of Neuchâtel, as in all Swiss cantons, create particular effects on the geographical mobility of students. A student residing in Neuchâtel who moves to Zurich to study might lose access to the Neuchâtel scholarship, as some cantons extend support even if the student changes canton for study reasons, others do not. A student from another canton who moves to Neuchâtel as a resident must wait to be registered in the population register before qualifying for cantonal scholarships.
Second element: the incentive to enroll in local institutions. Since each canton mainly funds studies at its own universities and training institutes, a student residing in Neuchâtel often receives higher amounts if they attend the University of Neuchâtel (UNINE) compared to enrollments in other Swiss cantons. This reflects the policy of encouraging local education, typical of Swiss cantonal governance.
### Concrete scenarios
Imagine a student whose family has an annual gross income that falls into the moderate need bracket of the canton: not poor, but not middle class either. [Calculate your potential gross salary](nav:calculator) to assess if your household might qualify. If they attend a low-cost bachelor's degree, the scholarship could cover 20-30% of the training costs. If they attend an expensive master's degree, it could rise to 40-50%. If they have excellent merit (high grades), some cantons award bonus amounts.
Another scenario: a student with a serious need situation (single-parent family, unemployment of a parent). Even with average academic merit, they might have priority over candidates with high merit but less need. The canton of Neuchâtel balances these two factors in the evaluation.
### How it changes over time
Swiss scholarships are partially indexed to inflation (not completely). When the cost of living increases, cantons can increase amounts and access thresholds, but often with a delay compared to real inflation. A student who accesses today with a certain amount might find, two years later, that their funding is no longer adequate, or that new selection criteria exclude them from continuation.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to apply
The procedure varies from year to year in Neuchâtel, but it follows a standard pattern.
First, check your residence. Make sure you are registered in the population register of the Canton of Neuchâtel. If you have just arrived from another canton or from abroad, you may have a waiting period (usually a few weeks from the first registration in the register before you qualify).
Second, download the form and the notice. Visit the website of the cantonal office of education and training (or Neuchâtel scholarship service) to find the annual notice. This document contains the deadlines, the application form, and the complete list of required documents.
Third, gather the documents: residence certificate, last bank statements or asset declarations, parents' pay slips for the last three months, copy of the family tax return (if available), enrollment certificate in the educational institution, academic merit document (official report card, academic transcripts).
Fourth, fill out the form carefully. Sections dedicated to personal data, family situation, declared income, current academic commitments. Be precise: errors or incomplete information can cause the application to be rejected.
Fifth, submit the application before the cantonal deadline. Deadlines are usually in the spring (for studies starting in September) or early autumn (for studies already started). There are no flexible deadlines: after the deadline, the application is not considered.
Sixth, wait for the evaluation by the canton. It usually communicates decisions within two or three months. If the application is rejected, you can appeal through the cantonal administrative procedure (appeal times vary depending on the canton).
### Where to find updated information
The competent office in Neuchâtel publishes notices and conditions on its official institutional website each year. Other useful resources include the websites of educational institutions (universities, high schools), which often have pages dedicated to scholarships from their own canton. Cantonal student associations also offer practical advice on procedures and deadlines.
In case of specific questions, contact the service directly: email and phone number are available online on the cantonal website. Do not delay: information and deadlines change every year, and delaying means risking missing the current year's notice.
### Implications for those changing cantons
If you study in Neuchâtel but come from another Swiss canton, it may be worth checking if your canton of origin also offers scholarships for studies conducted outside the canton. Some cantons do (if the training is not available locally), others do not. A cumulative scholarship from two cantons at the same time is rare, but possible under certain circumstances.
To evaluate if your economic situation qualifies for a scholarship, it is useful to first understand how much it costs to live in the Canton of Neuchâtel compared to other Swiss cantons, and what your actual tax and income situation is. Consult the [guide to the cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) for a comparative estimate and access the [tax return section](nav:tax-return) to clarify your certified gross income: this data will directly influence the evaluation of the cantonal office.
First day as a cross-border worker? Our [practical guide](nav:first-day) walks you from cantonal registration to your first paycheck.

item.title: Beloved Foundation: seventy requests received
item.description: The Beloved foundation received 70 requests from the victims of the Crans-Montana fire. Provides psychological, financial and rehabilitative support.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Beloved Foundation has received about 70 requests from fire victims - Has CHF 24 million from Valais, Vaud and private donors - Offers psychological, financial and rehabilitation support
## Key facts - **What**: Foundation established to assist victims of the Crans-Montana fire - When: 27 March (institution), 41 dead and 115 injured (New Year) - Where: Crans-Montana, Le Constellation bar (Canton of Valais) - Who: Christian Cardon (director), Doris Leuthard (president) - Amount: CHF 24 million from Valais, Vaud, municipality and private donors - Status: 70 requests received, no refusals so far
The Beloved Foundation, established on 27 March at the initiative of the Canton of Valais, has so far received about seventy requests for assistance from the victims of the fire at the Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana on New Year's Eve, which caused 41 deaths and 115 injuries. Director Christian Cardon, interviewed by Le Matin Dimanche, specifies that "for the moment there has been no rejection": some questions have already been approved, others remain under evaluation.
Several tens of thousands of francs have already been disbursed, Cardon reports. The foundation has a total endowment of 24 million francs, the result of donations and pledges from the Valais Canton, the Vaud Canton, the Municipality of Crans-Montana and private donors.
### Integrated support to victims and families
The scope of intervention of the foundation is wide: yes ### The coordination strategy and long-term needs
The foundation's operational model reflects an awareness of the complexity that accompanies a health and social emergency of this magnitude. LAV already guarantees a minimum level of assistance to victims of crime, but the case of Crans-Montana has highlighted how needs go far beyond standard services. The Beloved Foundation thus positions itself as a compensation tool, activating specific resources for situations that would otherwise remain uncovered.
This approach also takes into account the particular nature of the tragedy: the psychological and physical effects of the fire are not resolved in a few months. Many of the injured (115 according to the fire's balance sheet) face long rehabilitations, surgical interventions, physiotherapy. Costs not directly covered by the public health system (LAMal) or disability benefits can become burdensome for families, especially in areas with a high cost of living such as Valais. This is where the foundation steps in with targeted financial aid.
### Search for additional funding and future challenges
The search for additional funds beyond the already available 24 million is a clear signal that Leuthard and Cardon do not underestimate future challenges. As Leuthard declares: "Even if the financial endowment is substantial, in the face of the psychological and physical consequences of the tragedy, we will need additional resources to carry out our action over several years." The needs, in fact, "will evolve and persist in the long term."
Several members of the foundation's board of directors resigned in the initial phases. Leuthard explained to RTS that "perhaps some had underestimated the scope of the task. The work is arduous and heavy, but now we have a good operational team and an active and positive foundation council." In addition to organizational difficulties, Leuthard recognizes that "we were shocked to see such a catastrophe happen in Switzerland. But an accident can always happen." In the face of this, systematic work on building controls and structural improvements is necessary, an activity already underway that directly concerns the responsibilities of the Swiss Cantons and Municipalities in terms of risk prevention.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to submit a request to the foundation
The access system to the Beloved Foundation is designed to be inclusive, but it still requires a formal presentation of the application. Although the source does not specify all procedural details, it is clear that the foundation evaluates each request on a case-by-case basis. Christian Cardon has emphasized that so far no request has been rejected, a sign of the constructive approach of the entity.
Victims and their families who wish to access the support of the foundation should:
1. Identify the area of need: psychological support, financial aid, professional retraining (for young people), personal projects 2. Document the economic or psychophysical situation relevant to the request 3. Submit the application directly to the Beloved Foundation (contacts available at the Canton of Valais, the Municipality of Crans-Montana or through institutional channels) 4. Wait for the evaluation: Director Cardon has confirmed that some requests are approved immediately, others remain in a more in-depth analysis phase
The foundation coordinates its work with other public entities, primarily those managing LAV benefits. If a victim is entitled to compensation or subsidies already provided by federal law, the foundation will not duplicate these benefits but will intervene with additional resources where necessary. This approach ensures efficient use of available funds and the widest possible coverage.
### Perspectives and access to the labor market
For young people who need professional retraining, the foundation has already shown itself to be proactive. The requests received so far include cases of working-age people who, due to the injuries sustained, need professional reorientation or access to alternative training paths. This aspect is particularly relevant in Valais, where the local labor market requires rapid reintegration.
The Beloved Foundation ultimately represents a model of coordinated public and private response to a national-scale disaster. Victims and families who find themselves in situations of economic or psychological difficulty should inform themselves at the Canton of Valais, the Municipality of Crans-Montana, or directly at the foundation (through the official website or cantonal offices) to access the available funds and services. The fact that no request has been rejected so far suggests that resources are still available and the foundation remains committed to supporting those in need.
